title: The blind king's yes
hookLine: the city starts calling Yudhishthira its future king, and Duryodhana makes his father an offer: a holiday in Varanavata
tomorrow: can a warning hide in plain sight?

cards: Talk in the streets of Hastinapura: people are saying Yudhishthira should be king. He's fair, he's truthful, he's Pandu's eldest. Dhritarashtra is blind, so he was passed over before; why should his line rule now?

Word reaches Duryodhana, and it burns. The Mahabharata gives him a long, anguished speech to his father: if Yudhishthira takes the throne, the crown will pass down his line, and we and our children will be shut out.

teach.b: Duryodhana's plan is dressed up as a kindness. Send the Pandavas away, he tells his father, to the town of Varanavata, where a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva, is under way.
Let them enjoy themselves, out of the capital, out of the people's eyes. Dhritarashtra hesitates. Pandu was good to me, he says, and the people love his sons; how can I do this?
But he loves his own son, and in the end he agrees. So the old king calls his nephews in and speaks warmly of Varanavata.
Yudhishthira sees the purpose behind it, the text says, but he's alone and without friends at court, and he agrees. Then Duryodhana calls a minister named Purochana and gives him the real job.
Build the Pandavas a fine house out of lac and resin and other things that burn, plastered so it looks like any house. Earn their trust. And one night, while they sleep, set it on fire.
Notice who makes the plot possible.
The blind king, who knew it was wrong, hesitated, and said yes because the one asking was his son.
Hindu teaching has a word for this. Moha: delusion, the fog of attachment, one of the six enemies within, beside anger and greed. Moha isn't too little love.
It's love wrapped so tightly around what's mine that it can't see what's right.
Many teachers point to the very first line of the Bhagavad Gita, spoken by this same king years later: what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? My sons, and Pandu's.
His eyes were blind from birth; teachers read moha as the deeper blindness.

how: The bait in this story is a festival of Pashupati, a name of Shiva; Hindus still worship Shiva as Pashupati, and the Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu carries the name.

o: the king of Varanavata, who ruled for Dhritarashtra
the priest who led the Shiva festival in Varanavata
the minister sent to build a house that would burn

p: attachment that clouds right and wrong

s: he hesitated, remembering Pandu's goodness and the people's love for his sons, then gave in to his own son.
the house was meant to look ordinary
built of lac and resin and other things that burn, plastered over to look like any house.
it's love wrapped so tightly around 'mine' that it can't see what's right, like the blind king's for his son.

games.q: a classmate's dad swears his son would never cheat, with the screenshots right in front of him. by today's teaching, what's going on?
o: moha: love for his own clouding what's right, like Dhritarashtra's.
he's right; family should always believe family.
he just doesn't care about his son.
games.why: Dhritarashtra loved his son, knew the plot was wrong, and said yes anyway. Hindu teaching names that fog moha.

practice: Think of someone you love so much it's hard to see them clearly: a child, a sibling, a best friend, your own team. Recall one time you took their side before you knew the facts. Don't scold yourself.
The Gayatri mantra, said by Hindus every morning, asks for exactly this: a mind made clear. If you pray, ask for that. If you don't, just name the 'mine' honestly, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Purochana, the minister Duryodhana trusted to build a house of lac and resin in Varanavata, and to set it aflame.

orig.note: Sanskrit moha: delusion, the fog of attachment; one of the six enemies within.

carryVoice: Your line: moha, love that blinds. The blind king said yes. Tomorrow: can a warning hide in plain sight?

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Jatugriha Parva (the citizens praise Yudhishthira; Duryodhana's appeal; Dhritarashtra sends the Pandavas to Varanavata; Purochana's commission)
Bhagavad Gita 1.1 (Dhritarashtra asks what 'my sons' and the sons of Pandu did at Kurukshetra)
The six inner enemies (shadripu: kama, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, matsarya), a standard Hindu teaching, in general
